extraction.name: CommonsenseQA
extraction.description: CommonsenseQA is a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering. It contains 12,247 multiple-choice questions generated by extracting from ConceptNet multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept. Crowd-workers author multiple-choice questions that mention the source concept and discriminate between each of the target concepts, encouraging questions with complex semantics that often require prior knowledge. The best baseline based on BERT-large obtains 56% accuracy, well below human performance of 89%.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.publisher: Tel-Aviv University; Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
extraction.citeAs: Talmor, A., Herzig, J., Lourie, N., & Berant, J. (2019). CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was generated in a multi-step process: (1) Extracting subgraphs from ConceptNet, each with one source concept and three target concepts connected by the same relation. (2) Asking Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) crowd-workers to author three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), where all questions contain the question concept and each has a different target concept as its answer. (3) Crowd-workers add two additional distractors per question: one selected from ConceptNet (sharing the relation) and one formulated manually. (4) Verification by a disjoint group of workers, where each question is verified by 2 workers and only questions answered correctly by at least one worker are used. (5) Adding textual context by querying Google search for web snippets.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web API, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet knowledge base (Speer et al., 2017), which contains 32 million triplets with nodes representing natural language concepts and edges representing commonsense relations. Web snippets retrieved from Google search.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered: (1) Triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or relations already well-explored in NLP (e.g., IsA) were filtered out, leaving 22 relations. (2) Triplets where one of the concepts had more than four words or was not in English were filtered. (3) Triplets where the edit distance between concepts was too low were filtered. This resulted in 236,208 triplets. Triplets were then grouped into question sets containing three triplets sharing the same question concept and relation, yielding approximately 130,000 triplets (43,000 question sets).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: AMT workers were shown a question concept and three answer concepts for each question set and asked to formulate three questions, each containing the question concept and with one answer concept as the correct answer. Workers were instructed to avoid using words with strong relations to the answer concept. For each question, workers added two distractors: one selected from ConceptNet (sharing the relation to the question concept) and one formulated manually. A separate group of verifier workers then validated questions by either marking them unanswerable or selecting the correct answer. Each question was verified by 2 workers, and only questions answered correctly by at least one verifier were kept (filtering out 15% of questions).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Only annotators for which at least 75% of the questions they formulated passed verification were accepted. The verification process filtered out 15% of questions. 122 formulators contributed, though 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions. Human evaluation on 100 random questions by 5 workers (not involved in question generation) yielded 88.9% accuracy via majority vote.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question was verified by 2 workers during quality verification. Human evaluation used 5 workers per question on a 100-question sample.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes reporting bias (Gordon and Van Durme, 2013) as a motivation—commonsense knowledge is trivial to humans but seldom explicitly reported on the web. Question formulation was dominated by a small number of workers (10 workers formulated more than 85% of questions), which may introduce stylistic biases. The top question concepts are skewed toward 'Person' (3.1%), 'People' (2.0%), 'Human' (0.7%), etc.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to English. Only 22 ConceptNet relations were used, filtering out general relations. Questions are constrained to multiple-choice format with five candidate answers. Analysis of BERT-large errors shows low accuracy on questions involving negation/antonyms (42.8%), factoid knowledge (38.4%), fine granularity distinctions (35.4%), and conjunction of conditions (23.8%).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is split into training/development/test sets with an 80/10/10 split. Two types of splits are provided: (a) random split (primary split) and (b) question concept split where sets have disjoint question concepts. Use cases include training, validation, and testing of commonsense question answering models, as well as incorporating commonsense knowledge into NLU systems.
